executive_assessment.text: Parish-level composite vulnerability and capacity differ from direct flood exposure; coastal transport examples name Speightstown, Holetown, Bridgetown and Oistins.
Beryl evidence identifies fishing assets and women processors/vendors as affected, while recovery accounts and proposed infrastructure support do not demonstrate restored incomes.
Coastal participation and enforcement weaknesses are dated institutional findings. No supported climate-violence or reverse-FCV pathway was found in the reviewed sources.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2024 reports: The composite vulnerability ranking places Saint Michael and Saint Joseph highest, followed by Saint Andrew, Saint John and Saint Lucy among Barbados's 11 parishes.
Source dated 2024 reports: Island-capacity scores are highest in Saint James and lowest in Saint Joseph; Saint Andrew and Saint Lucy also rank near the bottom.

Source dated 2020-10 reports: The plan reports more frequent flooding after extreme rainfall raises disruption risk along coastal links among Speightstown, Holetown, Bridgetown and Oistins, affecting tourism and freight.
Source dated 2024-10-18 reports: The PID reports Beryl damaged 240 vessels, Bridgetown Port and marina breakwaters; 73% of hotels, apartments and guest houses and 40 houses also suffered damage.

Source dated 2024-10-18 reports: The Government mobilized partners to relocate vessels, clear debris and repair Bridgetown Port; it established a Fisheries Benevolent Fund to support fisherfolk livelihoods.

Source dated not stated reports: UNDP's Japan-funded project aims to upgrade select Bridgetown Fisheries Complex infrastructure and equipment, support affected livelihoods and strengthen the fishing community's disaster preparedness through capacity building.

known_gaps.text: No existing BRB country baseline directory was present in the assigned worktree.

No reviewed primary source links climate stress to armed conflict, violence or insecurity in Barbados, or documents conflict/insecurity disrupting climate adaptation; this is a search gap, not evidence of absence.

The ICZM plan's reported coastal user conflicts are linked to limited stakeholder participation, not explicitly to climate hazards or violence; the plan is dated 2020 and may not represent current institutional conditions.

Parish-level PDC composites are multi-hazard and do not reveal climate-specific household or social-group vulnerability within individual coastal sites; the coastal-transport corridor evidence lacks local flood counts.
The 2026 fisherfolk survey post does not disclose sample size or site-disaggregated results; underlying survey materials were not located.
The UNDP project page and World Bank PID report different Beryl vessel-damage estimates (>200 versus 240); neither estimate was reconciled against underlying damage records.
The IDB beach-erosion profile PDF exceeded the reader size limit and the 2026 Water Authority drought article returned 403; no claims rely on indexed-only content.
No mediated FCV chain is assembled: coastal-user conflicts are participation/governance context without a documented climate trigger.
Multi-hazard parish composites must not be presented as climate-specific rankings or household risk measurements.
